identity.title: Abrupt onset and abrupt termination of palpitations (vs gradual)

technique.how: Ask how the palpitations start and stop: 'like a switch' (instantaneous onset, sudden stop within one beat) versus building up and fading over minutes. Ask whether vagal manoeuvres (breath-holding, straining) terminate them, and what the patient was doing at onset (rest, exertion, anxiety).
technique.prerequisites: Patient must have experienced and be able to recall discrete episodes.

interpretation.positive_finding: Abrupt on/off palpitations, particularly if terminated by vagal manoeuvres, suggest a re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT/AVRT, atrial flutter) rather than sinus tachycardia; this is a pattern-recognition prior without a measured LR.
interpretation.negative_finding: Gradual onset and offset favour sinus tachycardia from anxiety, exertion, fever, anaemia or thyrotoxicosis, but does not exclude arrhythmia.
interpretation.pitfalls: The 2009 JAMA RCE found no significant accuracy for onset characteristics; patients often cannot time onset precisely and panic attacks may also feel abrupt. Duration <5 minutes slightly lowers arrhythmia likelihood (LR 0.38) in the same review.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: obtain ECG during symptoms or ambulatory/event monitoring for SVT; negative: does not exclude arrhythmia, still needs symptom-rhythm correlation if recurrent.

sources.citation: Thavendiranathan P, Bagai A, Khoo C, Dorian P, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with palpitations have a cardiac arrhythmia? JAMA. 2009;302(19):2135-2143.
Weber BE, Kapoor WN. Evaluation and outcomes of patients with palpitations. Am J Med. 1996;100(2):138-148.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use onset/offset character to exclude arrhythmia in patients with structural heart disease, syncope with palpitations, or an abnormal resting ECG.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Palpitations with syncope, chest pain, or haemodynamic compromise need immediate ECG and monitoring irrespective of onset pattern.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Subjective; the RCE notes most palpitation history items were studied in single small cohorts with wide confidence intervals.

extraction_notes: Anchor RCE (Thavendiranathan 2009, PMID 19920238) is not open access; its abstract lists the only significant history items (known cardiac disease, palpitations affected by sleep or at work, duration <5 min, panic disorder history, neck pounding) and states 'No other features significantly alter the probability of clinically significant arrhythmia', so no defensible LR for abrupt onset/offset exists from the accessible text and the record is not_quantified. Weber & Kapoor 1996 (the RCE's main primary cohort, 190 patients) is cited for the clinical-evaluation context; its abstract gives no onset-pattern accuracy. Searches 'palpitations sensitivity specificity arrhythmia history sudden onset termination' returned no primary accuracy study. Clinical use rests on textbook/guideline pattern recognition.
